title: VLAN: Vision-Language Accessible Navigation
claim: The same scene and obstacles yield different accessibility outcomes for different embodiments, so evaluation must be conditioned on the user.
layout: Central 3D scene with colored paths; obstacle cards left, legend panels right
description: A 3D-reconstructed street scene fills the center. It has a red goal flag at the top and several yellow start points at the bottom. Colored arrowed trajectories (blue, yellow-green, teal) run from the starts to the goal. Each trajectory is followed by a different agent: a drone, a wheelchair user, or a cane-using person. Obstacles are placed along the way: a traffic cone, a barrier, a tree and a ground hazard. On the left, four tilted cards show an obstacle crop with a red dashed box. Each card lists per-agent labels (Bypass, Passable, HighRisk, Blocked), with HighRisk and Blocked in orange and red. On the right, panels show navigation agent icons, mobility obstacle icons, and a text box explaining how outcomes differ by user. A small box at the top lists the accessible features (scene, agent, obstacle, trajectory). Xyz axes and Δx/Δy marks sit near the bottom.
caption: Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN) evaluates whether models can produce embodiment-specific navigation actions and accessibility predictions for a visual scene with same start-goal pair and obstacle layout. Since accessibility is conditioned on user mobility and perception, the same obstacle may induce distinct outcomes across users, ranging from passable to blocked.
abstract: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. Unlike goal-only evaluation, our benchmark measures physical safety and alignment with user-specific constraints via goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned metrics. We benchmark modern vision-language models and find they often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, and safety criteria across user profiles, suggesting accessibility-aware navigation requires dedicated datasets, tasks, and metrics beyond conventional embodied navigation evaluation. All data and code open-source at https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/VLAN.
